passage:
Monday: Maria was hanging clothes on the balcony in Goa when a peg dropped. Gargi toddled over, picked it up and held it high until Maria took it.
Wednesday: Maria came in with shopping bags in both hands. Gargi ran and pushed the half-closed door wide open, then went back to her blocks.
Saturday: Maria's spoon clattered off the table. Before anyone spoke, Gargi fetched it and handed it up, not waiting for a thank-you.

qa.q: What did Gargi do on Wednesday when Maria came in with shopping bags?
qa.a: She ran and pushed the half-closed door wide open, then went back to her blocks.

qa.q: Why do you think Gargi picks things up without being asked?
qa.a: Gargi seems caring and eager to help when Maria needs something, since Gargi does it without being asked or waiting for thanks.

qa.q: How can Maria encourage Gargi's helping without turning it into a reward game?
qa.a: She can warmly say what Gargi did, like "You opened the door for me," rather than offering sweets for each help.

qa.q: What would change if Maria only praised Gargi when she had asked her to help?
qa.a: Gargi might start helping only on request, and her natural, unasked kindness could fade.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up dropped items and helping without prompt or reward over several days.

passage: In their Bengaluru flat, Lakshmi Paati bent over the newspaper and her glasses slid off and skittered under the sofa. She sighed and began to lower herself to her knees. Nitin, two, dropped his toy truck, crawled flat under the sofa and came out holding the glasses by one arm. He pushed them into her hand. When her pen rolled off the table a moment later, he grabbed that too, then went straight back to his truck.

qa.q: Where did Lakshmi Paati's glasses slide?
qa.a: Her glasses slid off and skittered under the sofa.

qa.q: What might Nitin have noticed that made him drop his truck?
qa.a: He probably saw Paati sigh and start to kneel, and seemed to understand she needed help reaching the glasses.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi Paati respond to Nitin's help?
qa.a: She could thank him simply and warmly so he knows his help mattered, without making a fuss or offering a treat.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Paati see Nitin crawling under the sofa for her?
qa.a: She would likely feel grateful and touched that such a small child noticed her struggle and helped on his own. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a toddler spontaneously fetching dropped items for an elder without being asked.

passage:
"Oops, my keys!" Sunaina said as they hit the floor by the door.
Uday, who was pulling on one sandal, dropped it and waddled over. "Keys!"
"Oh, you got them?"
"Here, Mummy." He held them up with both hands.
"Thank you, Uday."
He was already back at his sandal. A minute later her dupatta slipped off her shoulder. Uday tugged the end and lifted it up to her.
"Look at you, noticing everything," she laughed.

qa.q: What was Uday doing when the keys fell?
qa.a: He was pulling on one sandal by the door.

qa.q: What does Uday going straight back to his sandal suggest about why he helped?
qa.a: It suggests he was simply happy to help rather than hoping for praise, since he went straight back without waiting for more thanks.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say next time to encourage this kind of help?
qa.a: She could name exactly what he did, such as "You picked up my keys," so he sees how his help made a difference.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Uday lifts her dupatta up to her?
qa.a: She would probably feel amused and warm, surprised at how quickly he notices small things she needs.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up dropped items for his mother without prompt or reward.

passage:
Playgroup note from Irfan Sir
Today Alka, who is two and a half, did something sweet. When a friend's crayon box fell and scattered, Alka went straight over, picked up every crayon and dropped them back in, one by one. Nobody asked her. Later she handed me my keys when they slipped off the table. 👍 I just said, 'Thank you, Alka,' and she went back to her puzzle.

qa.q: What did Alka hand to Irfan Sir later?
qa.a: She handed him his keys when they slipped off the table.

qa.q: What does Alka going back to her puzzle after being thanked suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she helped because she wanted to, not to get praise or a reward.

qa.q: What did Irfan Sir do well in his response?
qa.a: He thanked her simply without making a big fuss or giving a prize, which keeps the helping her own choice.

qa.q: How might the friend whose crayons fell see Alka?
qa.a: The friend may feel looked after and more likely to see Alka as kind and friendly.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler spontaneously helping by picking up dropped items without being asked.

passage: By the village well, Kishore Dada was washing his face, his gamchha draped on the stone edge. A gust blew it into the dust. Before he could bend, little Devika toddled over, grabbed the cloth in both fists and held it up to him, beaming. 'Dada, lo!' Nobody had told her to. He took it, laughed, and ruffled her hair. She was already running back to chase the hens.

qa.q: What did the gust blow into the dust?
qa.a: It blew Kishore Dada's gamchha off the stone edge into the dust.

qa.q: How did Devika seem to feel about helping Dada?
qa.a: She seemed happy and eager, beaming as she held the cloth up to him without anyone asking.

qa.q: How could adults encourage this kind of helping?
qa.a: They can notice it warmly, as Dada did with a laugh, without turning it into a task or a reward.

qa.q: How does Kishore Dada see what Devika did?
qa.a: He seems touched and amused that such a small child noticed and helped him on her own.

grounding: Shows a toddler assisting an elder without prompt or reward, set in an Indian village.

passage: At the small library in Copenhagen, Freya, the librarian, was carrying a stack of picture books when the top three slid off. Javier, twenty months, was sitting on the rug with his mother. Nobody asked him. He got up, toddled over, picked up one book with both hands and held it up to Freya. Then he fetched the second, and the third, and went straight back to the rug.

qa.q: How many books slid off Freya's stack?
qa.a: The top three.

qa.q: What might Javier have wanted when he held the book up to Freya?
qa.a: He seemed to want to help her, and maybe felt proud doing it, since no one asked or rewarded him.

qa.q: How could Freya respond to encourage this kind of helping?
qa.a: A simple warm thank you, using his name, is enough; no treat is needed.

qa.q: What is it like for Freya to be helped by a toddler?
qa.a: It is probably a touching surprise that brightens her day. 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler helping an adult pick up dropped books without being asked.

passage: I'm Thomas, from the house next door. On Sunday I saw Seema's grandmother hanging washing on the terrace when she knocked the peg tin over. Seema, who's about two, was playing with a bucket nearby. She stopped, looked, then started picking up the pegs one by one and dropping them back in the tin. Her grandmother hadn't said a word. When the tin was full, Seema carried it over with both arms and went back to her bucket.

qa.q: What did Seema's grandmother knock over?
qa.a: The peg tin.

qa.q: What does Seema going back to her bucket afterwards suggest?
qa.a: She seemed to help simply because she wanted to, not for praise, and felt content to return to play.

qa.q: How could Seema's grandmother show she noticed the help?
qa.a: Thank her warmly by name, so Seema knows her help mattered.

qa.q: How does Thomas see what Seema did?
qa.a: Thomas notices she helped without being asked and was not after any reward.

grounding: Shows a toddler spontaneously picking up spilled pegs for her grandmother, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Onam week in Kochi. First morning: Manjula dropped a basket of marigold petals while making the pookalam, and Simran, two, just watched. Third day: when petals spilled again, Simran squatted and scooped handfuls back into the basket without a word. Thiruvonam day: Manjula's hands were full with the payasam pot, and her slipper came off at the door. Simran picked it up and set it by her mother's foot.

qa.q: What did Manjula drop on the first morning?
qa.a: A basket of marigold petals.

qa.q: What might Simran have felt when she set the slipper by her mother's foot?
qa.a: Probably proud and pleased to be useful, since she did it without being asked.

qa.q: How could Manjula support Simran's new helping?
qa.a: Notice and thank her, and give her small jobs like sorting petals so she can keep helping.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had scolded Simran for touching the petals?
qa.a: Simran might stop offering help, feeling her efforts were unwelcome.

grounding: Shows a toddler starting to help her mother without being asked over a festival week.

passage: In the Holi rush at Sadar Bazaar, Mohit Chacha dropped his keys while paying for colour packets. Nobody noticed except Suraj, twenty months, standing by his leg. Suraj bent, picked up the keys with both hands, and held them up high. "Chacha!" Mohit looked down, surprised. "You found them? Thank you, Suraj!" Suraj grinned and went back to staring at the colours.

qa.q: What did Mohit Chacha drop?
qa.a: His keys.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when Chacha thanked him?
qa.a: Suraj felt pleased and proud, grinning.

qa.q: How could Chacha encourage this kind of helping?
qa.a: Thank him warmly and specifically, as he did, and let him help with small tasks.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when Suraj holds up the keys?
qa.a: Mohit was surprised and grateful, touched that a toddler noticed without being asked.

grounding: In a busy Holi market, a toddler spontaneously picks up his uncle's dropped keys.

passage:
"Where are my specs?" Kishore Dadu patted his kurta pockets. It was the week before Pongal, and brooms were everywhere.
Dhruv, twenty-two months, looked around, toddled to the sofa, and pulled the glasses from between the cushions.
"Dadu!"
"Dhruv! You found them?"
Dhruv held them out, then tried to put them on Dadu's nose himself.
"Gently, gently. Thank you, kanna."
"Dadu see?"
"Dadu sees everything now."
Dhruv clapped and went to pick up a broom that had fallen over.

qa.q: Where were Dadu's glasses?
qa.a: Between the sofa cushions.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when he clapped?
qa.a: Dhruv felt happy and proud of helping Dadu.

qa.q: What shows Dhruv's helping was spontaneous, and how can Dadu encourage it?
qa.a: Nobody asked him; he found the glasses and then picked up a fallen broom; Dadu can keep thanking him warmly.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel as Dhruv puts the glasses on his nose?
qa.a: Kishore probably felt amused and touched, grateful for the help even if it was clumsy.

grounding: Before Pongal, a toddler finds his grandfather's glasses and helps without being asked.

passage: Daycare note, December, rehearsal week for the Christmas play. I dropped a whole box of crayons while carrying the paper stars. Before I could bend, Lavanya (2) crouched and began picking them up, one by one, dropping them back into the box. Nobody asked her. When she finished, she handed me the box and went back to her star. I thanked her in front of the group, and two others started tidying too. I'll share this with her parents. — Thomas

qa.q: What did Thomas drop?
qa.a: A whole box of crayons.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt as she handed back the box?
qa.a: Lavanya probably felt content and helpful, calmly going back to her star afterwards.

qa.q: How did Thomas encourage helping in the group?
qa.a: He thanked Lavanya in front of everyone, which inspired others to help tidy.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel proud and happy to hear she helped without being asked.

grounding: A daycare note from Christmas rehearsal week records a toddler spontaneously picking up dropped crayons.

passage:
Winter sun warmed the terrace of the house near Gangtok. Ankita was hanging washing, and Pema, two, toddled after her.

A wooden peg fell from Ankita's hand and rolled under the bench.

Nobody asked her, but Pema crouched, reached under the bench, and pulled it out. She held it up to Ankita, arm stretched as high as it would go.

Ankita took it. "Thank you, Pema!" Pema went looking for another.

qa.q: Where did the peg roll?
qa.a: It rolled under the bench.

qa.q: How did Pema likely feel handing the peg to Ankita?
qa.a: Pema seemed proud and pleased to help, going to look for another.

qa.q: How can Ankita encourage Pema's helping?
qa.a: Thank her warmly and let her keep helping with small safe tasks like handing pegs.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when Pema brought the peg without being asked?
qa.a: Ankita would likely feel surprised and touched by her little helper.

grounding: A toddler spontaneously picks up a dropped peg and hands it back without being asked.

passage:
The first snow had fallen in Istanbul, and Nadia was walking Yara, two, home from the bakery.

Nadia's glove slipped out of her pocket and landed in the snow. She didn't notice.

Yara did. She stopped, bent over carefully in her puffy coat, picked up the glove, and trotted after her mother. "Mama! Mama!" She held it up.

Nadia turned, surprised. "My glove! Thank you, Yara."

qa.q: What fell out of Nadia's pocket?
qa.a: Nadia's glove slipped out of her pocket.

qa.q: How did Yara seem to feel as she trotted after her mother?
qa.a: Yara seemed eager and happy to help, calling out as she held up the glove.

qa.q: How could Nadia encourage Yara's helpfulness?
qa.a: Thank her warmly and let her carry something small, like the bread bag, on the way home.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel when Yara held up the glove?
qa.a: Nadia was surprised and grateful.

grounding: In the first snow, a toddler picks up her mother's dropped glove and returns it without being asked.

passage:
I'm Damini, and I'm fifteen. During Ganesh festival, Dadaji was sitting at the pandal and his walking stick fell over.

My cousin Nandini, who's two, was eating a laddoo. She put it down on her plate, went over, and tried to lift the stick. It was bigger than her. She dragged it to Dadaji and pushed it against his knee.

Nobody told her to. Dadaji patted her head. She went back to her laddoo.

qa.q: What was Nandini eating?
qa.a: Nandini was eating a laddoo.

qa.q: What might Nandini have felt as she dragged the stick to Dadaji?
qa.a: Damini can't know for sure, but Nandini seemed determined and caring, wanting to help Dadaji.

qa.q: How could the family encourage Nandini's helping?
qa.a: Thank her and notice when she helps others, so she keeps doing it.

qa.q: How might Dadaji feel when Nandini brought the stick?
qa.a: Dadaji was likely touched and pleased, patting her head.

grounding: A teenage cousin observes a toddler spontaneously bringing her grandfather's fallen stick without being asked.
